description: We are a team of Computer Engineering students from Bilkent University. We are highly motivated and have the technical skills to turn ideas into working software, with hands-on experience in software and game development. We're joining NASA Space Apps Ankara 2026 to build a project we're proud of.
summary:
Regolith is a co-op, first-person game about designing a space mission and building a colony, made for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (Space Mission Design Game). Players start in Mission Control. They choose a science goal, trade off launcher, transfer orbit, power, communications, instruments and cargo against a fixed budget, and take the design through NASA-style reviews (MCR -> PDR -> CDR -> FRR). Then they launch, land on real NASA terrain at Shackleton crater on the Moon or Jezero crater on Mars, and build an outpost from local resources. They drill ice, lay power and pipe networks, turn regolith into oxygen, metal and fuel, and send their data back to Earth over a link with real light-time delay.

Every design decision has a measurable effect later, on landing fuel, power, data return and the science result. Players learn how real missions are designed by facing the consequences of their own design. Up to four players work as a crew in the browser. They learn space systems engineering, in-situ resource use and the scientific method by doing them, not by reading about them.
details:
The game follows the full chain of a real mission: science need -> measurable requirements -> mission architecture -> design reviews -> launch -> surface operations -> data return to Earth -> evidence-based scientific conclusion. It covers four NASA mission segments:

- Mission design: In a shared Mission Control lobby, each crew role edits its own part of the design. A decision summary shows how each change affects arrival, science and the Earth link.

- Launch: A launch sequence with scrubs, ascent, trans-lunar or trans-Mars injection and course corrections. Pressing the key at the right moment for stage separation and fairing jettison affects the fuel left for landing.

- Surface: Players prospect with a spectrometer and core sampler, deploy structure kits and wire them into power grids and pipelines. Materials go through real multi-step processes at five workstations, such as making solar cells, PLA plastic from greenhouse biomass, and iron-air batteries. Players can fly the walkable lander to new sites, drive the LTV rover, and shelter from proton storms replayed from real solar flares.

- Ground: Data travels to Earth with real light-time delay and counts only when it arrives. Players buy Deep Space Network antenna time from an operations budget.

- User: An Earth science desk asks a science question, and players answer it with the evidence that actually reached Earth.

## What's real

- Terrain: NASA LRO LOLA 5 m/pixel elevation of the Shackleton rim, and an MRO HiRISE 1 m stereo model of the Jezero delta.

- Sunlight: horizon maps computed from that terrain. At the lunar pole the Sun circles the horizon, so solar power is ray-marched against the real ridges, and permanently shadowed craters are the only places ice appears.

- Physics and chemistry: real gravity, engine specific impulse and the rocket equation, plus real ISRU chemistry: electrolysis, molten regolith electrolysis, MOXIE and Sabatier.

- Live NASA data: DONKI solar flares, JPL Horizons, DSN Now, Launch Library 2 and APOD.

## Benefits and intended impact

Players learn by failing safely. An over-ambitious design runs short of fuel, power or bandwidth, and the game shows why. Co-op play mirrors how real mission teams work: someone flies while others build, and everyone has to sign off before launch. Because it runs in a desktop browser, students and classrooms can play without installing anything. The goal is to make systems engineering and planetary science feel concrete and exciting, and to inspire future mission designers.

## Tools and technologies

- Engine and language: Godot 4.5 and GDScript, with custom GLSL shaders for terrain lighting and the sky.

- Web and co-op: a WebGL 2 and WebAssembly browser build, with a server-authoritative co-op model over WebSockets/ENet that validates every request.

- Tooling: Python tools to build the terrain data (fetched from NASA PDS) and the web package; Node.js and Chrome for automated browser co-op tests; ffmpeg for gameplay footage.

- 3D models: NASA 3D Resources (Apollo LM, Perseverance, InSight, RASSOR, ISS parts and more), plus credited CC BY / CC0 models.

- Hardware: a standard Windows PC; players need only a modern desktop browser.

## Creativity

The game turns a full mission lifecycle, normally a long engineering process, into one continuous play session. It uses real NASA terrain and live data, so you play on real ground: the lighting and resources you see come from actual lunar and Martian data. The polar Sun circling the horizon becomes a gameplay mechanic. Crafting follows real manufacturing steps, and the science result depends on evidence that has to reach Earth.

## Factors the team considered

- Scientific accuracy: the game labels clearly what is simulated and what is real hardware.

- Ease of learning: a mission chain doubles as the tutorial, plus an interactive 15-step starter guide.

- Fairness and anti-cheat in co-op: the server checks materials and production.

- Save safety: saves are written atomically and can be recovered.

- Performance: the game runs well on browser hardware.

- Accessibility: players can join from a link with no installation.

- Licensing: NASA public-domain assets and credited open-licensed models only.
